title: Why does a Hibernate UPDATE set every column even when only one changed? How does dirty checking work, how does @DynamicUpdate fix it, and how can merge() accidentally overwrite columns with null?
shortTitle: Why does Hibernate UPDATE set every column?
topicTitle: Performance: Large IN, Dirty Checking, OSIV
keyPoints: By default Hibernate generates one static UPDATE per entity that sets every mapped column, reusing the same prepared statement.
Dirty checking compares each managed entity's current fields to its load-time snapshot to decide whether an UPDATE is needed.
@DynamicUpdate generates the UPDATE at runtime with only the changed columns, reducing unnecessary writes.
Use @DynamicUpdate selectively on wide tables or tables with triggers; it has a small cost of per-flush SQL generation.
merge() copies the entire state of a detached entity onto the managed entity, so null fields overwrite existing database values.
The merge null-overwrite trap is especially dangerous when mapping an API request DTO directly onto an entity and merging.
The safe pattern for partial updates is to load the managed entity and set only the fields you intend to change.

s1_definition.oneliner: Default UPDATE sets all columns for statement reuse; `@DynamicUpdate` writes only changed columns; `merge()` copies the entire detached state, so null fields can blank existing data.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Static UPDATE** -- Hibernate caches one pre-generated UPDATE per entity that sets every mapped column, so even a single field change writes all columns.
- **Dirty checking** -- at flush, Hibernate compares each managed entity's current fields to its load-time snapshot; if anything differs, the static UPDATE runs.
- **@DynamicUpdate** -- tells Hibernate to generate the UPDATE at runtime with only the dirty columns, reducing unnecessary writes.
- **Statement reuse** -- the default static UPDATE can be prepared once and reused, cooperating well with the JDBC statement cache.
- **merge() null-overwrite** -- `merge()` copies the entire detached entity's state onto the managed entity, so any field that is null on the detached object overwrites the database value with null.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's update form always has every field printed on it, and Rajesh re-writes Priya's entire record -- name, address, phone, balance -- every time even if only the phone number changed. It is faster to use one pre-printed form than to custom-print a new form each time. But if Priya hands in a form where she only filled the phone number and left name and address blank, and Rajesh copies the whole form over the record, the blanks wipe out her existing name and address.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Dirty Checking + UPDATE generation:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Persistence Context                         │
  │                                              │
  │  Snapshot:          Current:                 │
  │  name = 'Priya'     name = 'Priya'   (same)  │
  │  balance = 50000    balance = 50000  (same)  │
  │  phone = '1111'     phone = '9876'   CHANGED │
  │  status = 'ACTIVE'  status = 'ACTIVE'(same)  │
  └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                         │
           ┌─────────────┴────────────────┐
           │                              │
     Without @DynamicUpdate        With @DynamicUpdate
           │                              │
     UPDATE accounts              UPDATE accounts
     SET name=?,                  SET phone=?
         balance=?,               WHERE id=?
         phone=?,
         status=?
     WHERE id=?
     (all columns)                (only changed)
```

```text
  merge() null-overwrite trap:

  Database row:              Detached entity:
  ┌─────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────┐
  │ name = 'Priya'  │       │ name = null     │
  │ balance = 50000 │  ◄──  │ balance = null  │  merge copies
  │ phone = '1111'  │       │ phone = '9876'  │  ALL fields
  │ status = 'ACTIVE'│      │ status = null   │
  └─────────────────┘       └─────────────────┘

  Result: name, balance, status WIPED to null!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
By default Hibernate generates one static UPDATE per entity that sets every mapped column, even when only one field changed. This is intentional: preparing one statement once and reusing it is cheaper than building custom SQL on every flush, and it cooperates with the JDBC statement cache. Dirty checking decides whether to update by comparing the current state to the load-time snapshot; the static UPDATE decides what columns to include.

`@DynamicUpdate` tells Hibernate to generate the UPDATE at runtime with only the dirty columns, which is valuable on wide tables, tables with column-level triggers, or tables where unnecessary writes cause problems. Apply it selectively because it loses the reusable prepared statement and adds per-flush SQL generation cost.

The separate and more dangerous issue is the merge null-overwrite trap. `merge()` copies the entire detached entity's state onto the managed entity, so if you build an entity from an API request that only set the phone and left name and balance null, merge copies those nulls and wipes the existing data. At National Bank of India, a profile update API did exactly this and blanked customers' names. The fix is to load the managed entity and set only the fields you intend to change, letting dirty checking persist the partial update safely.

Remember one sentence: the default all-columns UPDATE is for statement reuse, `@DynamicUpdate` writes only changed columns for wide tables, and never merge a partially-populated entity because null fields overwrite existing data.
